title: Best Affirmation Apps for Anger and Irritability in 2026
description: The best affirmation apps for anger and irritability in 2026, compared by whether their sentences lower arousal rather than raise it, whether you can write a self-distanced line at a believable size, whether they reach you in the hot minute before the reply is sent, and what they cost over a year — with the venting, self-distancing and arousal research stated at its real size.
markdown:
By Anicca · November 2026

"Best affirmation app" is the wrong question when what you actually have is not a shortage of calm but a reply already typed. Someone has been careless with your work, or dismissive in a meeting, or slow in the lane you needed, and the heat arrives before the thought does: jaw tight, shoulders up, the message in the box getting sharper with every edit — and each edit feels like honesty. Or the spike is smaller and more frequent than that: the irritation that flares at a partner's tone, a child's noise, a notification, until you are snapping at the people who did not cause it and spending the evening apologising for a sentence that took four seconds to say. That minute — between the provocation and the send, the snap, the slammed door — is what changes what an app has to do, and it rules out most of what affirmation apps sell. A person in anger does not need a louder inner voice. The inner voice is already loud. Nor do they need to "let it out": the best evidence we have says venting while rehearsing the provocation makes people angrier and more aggressive, not less. What can help, modestly and honestly, is narrower: words that lower the body's heat rather than raise it, written at a distance and a size you can believe — "he was careless with the deadline; the reply can wait ten minutes" rather than "I am a calm and peaceful person" said through clenched teeth — arriving in the hot minute, before the send, from an app that never converts a bad-tempered week into a broken streak. The apps below are therefore not ranked by who motivates you most. Motivation is arousal, and arousal is the problem. They are ranked by what still helps, honestly, when the reply is typed, the thumb is hovering, and the person you will have to apologise to is already in the room. This comparison follows the same form as our roundups of the best affirmation apps for anxiety, for sleep and racing thoughts at night, for self-esteem and low self-worth, for stress and overwhelm, for overthinking and rumination, for imposter syndrome and the fraud feeling at work, for perfectionism and the flawless-or-failure loop, for social anxiety and the replay after conversations, for burnout and exhaustion that rest does not fix, for a breakup and the urge to check their profile, for grief after the death of someone you love, for depression and persistently low mood, for people-pleasing and the fear of disapproval, for health anxiety and the search-check-reassure loop, for loneliness and the quiet room at night, for OCD and intrusive thoughts, and for shame and guilt and the replay that turns an act into a verdict, re-aimed at anger and irritability and the sixty seconds in which a feeling becomes a sentence someone else has to live with.

*Disclosure: Anicca, the app listed sixth here, is made by the team behind this site. It is not ranked first. No app paid to be here. Prices and ratings are from the US App Store listings when we last checked them on November 20, 2026; check the store page for your country. Two boundaries before the list itself. First: anger is an emotion, not a diagnosis, and it is often information — about a boundary crossed, a workload that is not survivable, a value that matters to you. The aim of this page is not to make you unbothered by things that should bother you; it is to keep the feeling from choosing the words, the volume and the timing. Second: no app on this page is a treatment for anything, including our own app. Where anger arrives as rage you cannot interrupt, where it is damaging your relationships, your work or your safety — or someone else's — that is a reason to talk to a clinician, and structured anger treatment has more support behind it than any app here. In a crisis, use your local emergency number now — in the US, call or text 988, or 911 in an emergency; in Japan, call 110 or 119 in an emergency. What follows is a comparison of self-help tools for the hot minute, written for people who are also, where they need it, getting real help.*

## How we judged these, for anger and irritability specifically

1. **Does it turn the heat down, or up?** This is the first filter, and most affirmation content fails it. Anger is not only a thought; it is physiological arousal — heart rate, tension, pressure — wearing a thought as its explanation. A 2024 meta-analysis of 154 studies found that activities which decrease arousal reduced anger and aggression, while activities which increase arousal were ineffective overall (Kjærvik & Bushman, 2024). Read against that finding, the register of an app's sentences matters as much as their content. Hype — triumph, dominance, "crush it", becoming unstoppable — is arousal in a positive costume, and in the hot minute it keeps the body at the temperature where the sharp reply feels proportionate. Sentences that rank here are the cooling kind: slow, plain, permissive about time — "this can wait ten minutes", "nothing has to be answered at this temperature". Apps whose default voice is a motivational speaker rank below apps whose voice could pass for a steady colleague.

2. **Can you write a distanced sentence, at a believable size?** The laboratory version of the skill this page needs is self-distancing: reflecting on a provocation as an observer — a fly on the wall — rather than reliving it through your own eyes. Provoked participants who did this had fewer aggressive thoughts, felt less angry, and behaved less aggressively than those who reflected self-immersed (Mischkowski, Kross & Bushman, 2012). A sentence you write yourself can be built at that distance — in the third person, or with your own name: "Daniel is furious about the deadline, and Daniel can answer at four" — in a way a fixed library sentence, written in the first person at the temperature of its author's best day, usually is not. Size matters for the same reason it matters everywhere in this series: Wood, Perunovic and Lee (2009) found that people with low self-esteem who repeated a large positive self-statement felt worse, because the gap summoned the counter-evidence. In anger the gap is a provocation of its own — "I am calm" is, mid-spike, simply false, and the mind argues. Apps that let you write, record and shrink a sentence rank above fixed libraries of large ones.

3. **Does it reach you in the hot minute, before the send?** Anger is fast and it is timed: the spike arrives with the message preview, the tone in the kitchen, the brake lights ahead. Its action urges — send, snap, correct, win — all complete within a minute, on the same phone the app lives on. The practical test is therefore timing and friction. A sentence already on your lock screen, or one press of play, can put ten minutes between the provocation and the reply — can turn "send it now, sharper" into "read the line first; the message will still exist at four o'clock, in a better version". An app that needs a programme, a session or a setup project arrives after the apology is already owed. Note what this criterion is not: it is not a venting channel. An app that invites you to rehearse the offence — to type the grievance out in full, at heat — is, on the evidence in the research section, feeding the flame it claims to extinguish.

4. **What does it cost, and what does a bad-tempered month cost you?** Learning to pause is measured in months, not in a trial week, and a habit study at University College London found a new behaviour took a median of 66 days to feel automatic, with a range of 18 to 254 days (Lally et al., 2010). Judge every app on the long window: what it costs over a year, and whether returning after three irritable weeks — weeks in which you did not open it, because opening things calmly was exactly what was hard — feels like resuming or like one more failure to explain. An app that greets absence with a broken streak has, for this reader, simply added a second offence to be angry about.

## The six at a glance

## 1. Believe: Best for writing the distanced sentence yourself, in your own voice

Believe takes first place here because question 2 is the whole game on this page, and Believe is the only app on this list built around letting you set the content of the claim yourself. You can **write your own affirmations**, **record them in your own voice**, and say them to your own face in the **Soul mirror**. That is how a sentence survives contact with a provocation. Not "I am a calm and peaceful person", which the spike will dismantle in seconds, but the line written at observer distance, on a steadier day, in the grammar the research supports: your name, the fact, the permission to wait — "he is angry because the work was dismissed in front of the team; the reply he sends at four will be better than the one he sends now, and sending nothing yet is also a reply". Its listing organises words by the moment you are in, and the named categories include **self-love** and **relationships**, alongside confidence before a hard day, calm before sleep, gratitude, mornings, work, study, health, money, mindfulness and personal growth, and its current listing adds a free "Mental Health" category. **Timed sessions** with music and calming sounds give one line room to land, and widgets and scheduled reminders cover the timing of question 3 — a reminder set for the commute, or for the hour the difficult colleague usually writes, is a sentence you arranged before the heat arrived. Write the lines cool, write them about the next ten minutes rather than about your character, and let the mirror be practice in being looked at — by yourself, at a distance — rather than a performance of serenity you do not feel.

Believe launched in June 2021 and showed **4.9 stars from 379 US ratings** when we checked on November 20, 2026. Its US listing shows Believe Premium+ at **$3.99 a month** and a **lifetime option at $69.99** among its in-app purchases.

### Where it falls short

The crowd is elsewhere — 379 ratings against I am's hundreds of thousands. If social proof is your evidence, the evidence is not here. Believe also tracks consistency with practice medals, which cuts directly against question 4: for most people medals are decoration, but if a broken streak would become one more thing to be irritated about, use the sessions and ignore the medals entirely. And the writing, the recording and the mirror all ask something of you up front, on a steadier day — including, for a person whose anger turns inward as often as outward, the hardest editorial decision on this page: the sentences have to be written about the situation and the wait, not as a prosecution of the other person rehearsed in a calmer voice, because a grievance recorded and looped is rumination with production values. That is why Innertune, which asks for one press, is second on this page.

## 2. Innertune: Best for sentences that arrive with one press while the heat falls

Innertune is the app for the moment when question 2 cannot even be attempted because the spike is already loud and the thumb is already moving. Its core practice requires, at the moment of use, exactly one press. Its listing opens with "Stop the negative thought spiral", builds **a personalised playlist for your exact situation** from **77,000 affirmations across 550+ playlists**, and is built to run while you sleep, work or relax. For anger and irritability, that passivity has one specific, honest use, and it is the use the meta-analysis predicts will work: press play instead of send, and let a slower voice occupy the channel while the body's heat — which is a physical event with a physical half-life — falls. What you do in those minutes is the point: the playlist is a timeout with a purpose, and the purpose is returning to the message when the reply you write is the one you would have written an hour later. Premium lists **19 voices including an ASMR option**, your own-voice recording if you want it later, binaural and sleep beats, a night mode and offline downloads. Its listing names its targets as anxiety and racing thoughts, sleep and restless nights, self-doubt and confidence, and breaking negative thought patterns — the neighbourhood of the spike, even if not its name.

Innertune showed **4.8 stars from 12,174 US ratings** when we checked on November 20, 2026. Its US listing shows premium plans including **$29.99 a year** and **$9.99 a month** among its in-app purchases.

### Where it falls short

Listening can become avoidance with good production. If pressing play turns into a way of never sending the reply that is owed — the boundary, the correction, the plain "that did not work for me" — the app has stopped being a timeout and become a hiding place, and anger deferred without ever being spoken tends to return at a worse address. Check a playlist's tone on a steadier day, too: a personalised playlist is still not a sentence sized to your belief, and any track whose register is conquest — winning, dominating, rising above them — is question 1's arousal in costume, and will keep the temperature it claims to lower. Skip those tracks. And Innertune is a subscription to listening, indefinitely; if what you need is words you eventually own without the app, start with Believe above.

## 3. I am: Best for a different sentence on the lock screen, at scale

I am is the category default, and its listing starts from a neighbouring observation: "How many negative thoughts have been repeating in your mind?" Its answer is placement and scale. On the App Store since 2014, **4.8 stars from 739,813 US ratings** when we checked on November 20, 2026, it lets you choose daily intentions and set **reminders to be delivered throughout the day**, with widgets and lock-screen lines in a library large enough that the sentence rarely repeats. For anger and irritability, the practical value is interruption at the exact surface where the send gets decided: the lock screen is where the provoking message previews, where the thumb is already authenticated and ready. A different sentence already there — before you open the thread and start drafting at heat — is question 3 done with zero effort, in the seconds where "wait ten minutes" is still possible. Set one reminder for the hour your spikes usually start, because that is when this page's reader will meet it. Premium is listed at **$59.99 a year** and **$14.99 a month**, with a **lifetime option at $89.99**, on its US store page.

### Where it falls short

The relationship is one-directional. You receive; you rarely make. There is no mirror, no voice recorder and no way to shrink a sentence until it is believable or rewrite it at observer distance, so the library's size works against questions 1 and 2 as often as for it: much of the category's general language leans toward achievement, dreams, ambitions and abundance — its listing speaks of verbally affirming your dreams and ambitions and becoming what you believe, and of ensuring every day is an amazing day. Read against question 1, that register is heat, not cooling: on a spike, a large sentence about your amazing, unstoppable self does not lower the temperature at which the sharp reply feels right — and against question 2, "I am calm" at maximum volume is the exact sentence Wood and colleagues' warning is about. And nothing in the app helps you do the thing anger is actually for, once it has cooled: name the problem plainly, once, to the person who can change it. Use I am for interrupting the spike with sheer variety and placement. For words written at a distance, it does not compete with the two apps above it.

## 4. Gratitude: Best for a written record of what actually happened

Gratitude is built from a private gratitude journal with prompts, a vision board, Daily Zen content, and affirmations you can **listen to or read**, write yourself, set to music and record in your own voice. For anger and irritability, the journal is the active ingredient — used in one specific way, and it is not the way the app's name suggests. Do not use it to count blessings, and do not use it in the hot minute at all. Use it afterwards, at a cooler temperature, as the record the rehearsing mind never keeps. Anger edits memory in a particular direction: it keeps the worst sentence in high resolution, deletes the provocation's context and your own part in the escalation, and stores the episode as evidence in a prosecution that reopens at the next spike. A dated line, kept brief and factual — "criticised in the 10:00 meeting; drafted the reply at 10:05, sent the shorter one at 10:20; she answered the question that was actually asked; no apology owed either way" — is written evidence, in your own hand, that the episode had edges, a temperature curve and an ending. Kept over weeks, that record is also how a pattern becomes visible at all: the same hour, the same meeting, the same empty stomach — which is information no affirmation can give you, and the only kind that changes the conditions rather than the wording. Its prompts and reminders lower the cost of starting, and the listing stresses that the journal is completely private — which matters here, because a record of your worst minutes written for an audience would be performed, not kept. It showed **4.9 stars from 44,996 US ratings** when we checked on November 20, 2026, and its US listing shows an annual pro plan at **$29.99** and a monthly plan at **$4.99**. It has been on the App Store since 2018.

### Where it falls short

The frame is gratitude, and the frame is a risk. On the evening after a real injustice, an app organised around counting good things can feel like an instruction to be thankful instead of accurate — and anger at something genuinely wrong is not an ingratitude problem. Keep the entries factual — the trigger, the wait, what was sent, what happened — and let the app's sunnier framing stay unused. The vision board and manifestation content point the wrong way for the same reason: a board of the triumphant future self is question 1's heat in picture form. There is a second, sharper warning specific to this page: a journal entry written at heat, rehearsing the offence in full detail, is the rumination condition from Bushman's experiment with a date on it. The record only works written afterwards, briefly, and closed. And like Believe, its strongest use here — the episode record — is a use you bring to it, not the use it advertises. If the name of the app itself irritates you in this season, that reaction is information; skip to Innertune or Believe.

## 5. ThinkUp: Best for your own voice saying the cooled line, on a loop

ThinkUp's core idea is the one your brain is built to trust: your own voice. You select affirmations from an expert-approved list or use them as inspiration to **create your own**, **record them in your own voice**, add an image that inspires you, set them to music, and loop the programme with notifications to listen daily. For anger and irritability, the own-voice recording is the real offer, for the same reason Believe ranks first: a sentence you wrote, at a distance you chose, said in the voice that lives in your head anyway, has a chance of being believed at heat that a stranger's serenity does not. Record the programme for the specific hour that costs you — the commute, the meeting's aftermath, the first ten minutes at home — because spikes are rarely general; they have times of day and doorways. And build the programme the way question 2 requires: let its lines name the situation and the wait, in order — "the message exists; it will exist at four; the reply sent at four is the one I stand behind; nothing about this hour is an emergency unless someone is unsafe" — so the loop ends with the temperature lower rather than with a larger claim about who you are. It has been on the App Store since 2014 and showed **4.7 stars from 7,524 US ratings** when we checked on November 20, 2026. Its US listing shows plans including **$7.99 a month**, **$39.99 a year** and a **lifetime option at $99.99** among its in-app purchases.

### Where it falls short

The framing around that recording is achievement language: its listing opens by asking what stops you from achieving goals or becoming who you want to be, and builds toward motivation, prosperity and success, including manifestation. Read against question 1, that vocabulary is pointed the wrong way for this feeling — you are not failing to become someone; you are trying not to send a sentence at the temperature it was drafted, and the work is cooling, not becoming. The loop format carries the warning from the research section in its strongest form: a programme whose lines rehearse the grievance — even in "empowered" language — played until you feel ready to respond, can quietly become rehearsal for the confrontation, and rehearsal at heat is what Bushman's rumination group did with a punching bag. Keep it short, keep it about the wait, and let some evenings end with the reply sent once, plainly, and no programme at all: that sending is the practice working, not failing. The programme model also assumes setup and daily listening discipline; building it is a project, and projects belong on the steadier days. Used narrowly — one recorded programme, your words, distanced, played in the hour that costs you — it earns its place.

## 6. Anicca: One short card, no streak, nothing to fall behind on

Anicca is our app, and it is listed last because on the evidence available today, last is where it belongs on this page. What it does is narrow: its listing describes it as **made for anxious, overthinking minds**; you **pick a focus — self-love and confidence are among those named** — and a new affirmation appears on your **Lock Screen every day**, with short cards you can swipe through at your own pace, save, copy or share, across 8 background themes, in six languages. There is no streak to break, no programme to build, no journal to keep up, and nothing that counts an irritable week against you — which, against questions 3 and 4, is the one thing it does exactly right for this feeling: it cannot become one more provocation, one more debt, or one more thing to be angry about, and it can be left alone for as long as you need and resumed without explanation. It does not ask you to face a mirror, write a record, or say anything aloud. On this page, that lightness is a feature, not a slogan. It is iPhone only.

The numbers, stated plainly because this page checks everyone else's: Anicca showed **5.0 stars from 1 US rating** and **4.5 stars from 48 ratings in Japan** when we checked on November 20, 2026. Its US listing shows premium at **$14.99 a month** and **$59.99 a year**. One rating is not social proof of anything, and this page will not dress it up as such.

### Where it falls short

Almost everywhere this page measures. There is no anger or irritability category, no way to write your own words or record your own voice, and no way to rewrite a sentence at observer distance until it stops arguing with the spike — the exact ability question 2 ranks first. Nothing in it times a sentence to the hot minute, keeps the episode record, or helps you tell information from temperature — which is the whole skill this feeling requires. Its named focuses are self-love and confidence, which are neighbouring needs, not this one, and some of its general positive language is larger, and hotter, than a spiking minute can hold — the arousal warning and the Wood et al. warning both apply to our own sentences too. If the spike itself is the thing, Believe and Innertune above are built closer to it, and the research section below matters more than any app on this page. Anicca fits a narrower moment: you want one kind line, already on the lock screen where the provoking message also previews, that asks nothing, counts nothing and raises nothing, from an app small enough to be honest about what it is.

## Also worth knowing: Mantra

Mantra, around since February 2017, showed **4.8 stars from 34,494 US ratings** when we checked on November 20, 2026. Its listing opens from the same observation as this page — "Our brains are wired to repeat negative feelings if fed with negative thoughts" — and is built around a daily affirmation you hold with, plus the ability to **read as many affirmations as you like by swiping**, across **30+ categories**, with smart daytime and bedtime reminders. Its current listing also lets you **add your own affirmations and record your voice**, which moves it closer to question 2 than a pure library. Its US listing shows a monthly plan at **$4.99** and annual plans including **$29.99** among its in-app purchases. It is a credible middle option — a large, established library with a light daily ritual — and the swipe-to-keep-reading form suits the restless hot minute when your hands need something to do that is not finishing the draft. What keeps it off the main list for this page is focus: its framing is general positivity and manifestation rather than the specific discipline this feeling needs, so its own-words tools arrive inside a library whose default sentences still need the steadier-day tone check described under Believe — keep the ones that name a wait and a next step, rewrite or skip the ones that announce victory.

## What the research does — and does not — say

Three findings decide how to use this list, and the first one is about heat. Kjærvik and Bushman (2024) meta-analysed **154 studies with 184 independent samples and 10,189 participants**, testing activities that increase arousal against activities that decrease it. The arousal-decreasing activities — deep breathing, relaxation, mindfulness, meditation, slow-flow yoga, progressive muscle relaxation, taking a timeout — **decreased anger and aggression (g = −0.63)**, with effects that held across genders, ages and cultures, in laboratories and in the field, in groups and individually, and whether delivered in person or digitally. The arousal-increasing activities — hitting a bag, jogging, cycling and the rest of the "blow off steam" family — were **ineffective overall (g = −0.02)**, and jogging in particular tended to increase anger. Hold the limit as firmly as the numbers: these are average effects across many short interventions, mostly measured in minutes and hours, not a promise about your worst day, and a meta-analysis of activities is not evidence that any particular app delivers them well. What it supports is question 1, stated as plainly as the data allows: in the hot minute, choose what cools. An app is, at best, a delivery vehicle for a timeout — and a vehicle whose own voice raises arousal is driving the wrong way.

Second, venting is not a loophole in that finding; it is the finding's oldest experiment. Bushman (2002) angered participants with insulting feedback, then assigned them to hit a punching bag while thinking about the person who had provoked them, to hit the bag while thinking about becoming physically fit, or to sit quietly with no bag at all. Catharsis theory predicted the first group would purge the anger. The opposite happened: **the rumination-and-venting group felt angriest and behaved most aggressively** afterwards, the distraction group sat in between, and **doing nothing at all was more effective than venting**. Read it honestly: one laboratory paradigm, students, noise blasts as the measure of aggression — not your marriage or your workplace. What it supports is narrower and still decisive for this page: the combination that makes anger worse is rehearsal plus expression at heat. Any app feature that invites you to type the grievance out in full, record the furious version, or "get it out" inside the app is building that combination a home. The record described under Gratitude is written afterwards, briefly, at a cooler temperature, for exactly this reason — and the distinction between the two kinds of writing is the distinction between the groups in this experiment.

Third, distance works in the heat of the moment, not only in hindsight. Mischkowski, Kross and Bushman (2012) provoked participants in the laboratory — berated over an intercom during a timed task — and then had them reflect on the scene for 45 seconds from a self-distanced perspective ("watch the event unfold from a distance, as if it were happening to the distant you"), a self-immersed perspective, or with no instruction. In the first experiment, with **94 students**, the self-distanced group showed **fewer aggressive thoughts and less angry feeling** than both other groups. In the second, with **86 students**, self-distancing also produced **less aggressive behaviour** toward the provoker. Hold every limit: two laboratory experiments, student samples, a staged provocation, minutes of follow-up — not evidence about chronic anger, trauma, or any app. What it supports is only the grammar of question 2: the same event, reflected on as an observer rather than relived as the protagonist, is measurably cooler — which is why this page ranks the apps that let you write the sentence yourself, in your name rather than your fury, above the libraries that write it for you.

Fourth, the size of the sentence is not a detail; it is the mechanism of failure. Wood, Perunovic and Lee (2009) showed in two experiments that participants with low self-esteem who repeated the positive self-statement "I'm a lovable person", or focused only on how it was true, **felt worse** than those who did not repeat it or who were allowed to consider how it was both true and not true — while participants with high self-esteem benefited slightly. The authors' own warning names the exact sentences this feeling attracts: outlandish, unreasonably positive self-statements may harm the very people they are designed for. "I am calm, I am peaceful, nothing bothers me", repeated at a spike, is that sentence wearing this page's colours: the mind cross-examines it against the evidence of the jaw, the shoulders and the draft, and returns a hotter verdict. Any app whose default move is a global claim about the self must be used, if at all, with its own-words tools and its smallest, most situational sentences — and a sentence that leaves you hotter is not a sentence to push through. It is a sentence to shrink, distance, or drop.

The boundary, stated plainly. Anger and irritability, by themselves, are not diagnoses, and nothing on this page is a treatment for any condition, including our own app. But either can sit inside larger things. If anger arrives as rage you cannot interrupt; if you are frightening people, breaking things, or damaging the relationships and work you most value; if it arrives with persistent low mood, trauma memories, substance use, or thoughts of harming yourself or someone else — that is a conversation for a clinician, or, in a crisis, your local emergency number or crisis line now (in the US, call or text 988, or 911 in an emergency; in Japan, 110 or 119 in an emergency). And the boundary runs in the other direction too: anger is sometimes the accurate reading of a situation — a boundary actually crossed, a workload actually impossible, a wrong actually done to you. Cooling the minute is not the same as accepting the condition. The cooled reply can still say no, still name the problem, still leave. Structured human help has more support behind it than any app on this page, and so does the plain sentence, sent once, at a temperature you chose.

The habit research points the same way as in our other comparisons. Lally et al. (2010) found a new behaviour took a median of 66 days to feel automatic, with a range of 18 to 254 days. A counter-practice — noticing the spike, letting the heat fall, sending the shorter reply — is still being built in month two, which is why question 4, what it costs over a year and what an irritable month costs you, outranks every feature list. A smaller app that costs nothing to resume beats a complete app you stopped opening because resuming it felt like one more thing to fail at, angrily.

## How to choose

- **You want words that are actually yours — distanced, written by you, at your size, in your voice, said to your own face:** Believe.
- **The spike is already loud and you need sentences that arrive with one press, while the heat falls and the draft stays unsent:** Innertune.
- **You want the biggest library and the most social proof, interrupting on your lock screen where the provoking message previews:** I am.
- **Writing down what actually happened — the trigger, the wait, what was sent, the outcome — is how you push back against the prosecution's edit:** Gratitude.
- **Your own voice on a loop is the requirement, and you have a steadier week coming in which to set it up for the hour that costs you:** ThinkUp.
- **You want one short card, on the focus you chose, with no streak to break and nothing that counts an irritable week against you:** Anicca.
